sources.entry: Rustrak - Error tracking server compatible with Sentry SDKs, using 32 MB of memory at idle with SQLite storage. (Source Code) GPL-3.0 Rust/Docker

summary.one_liner: Rustrak is a self-hosted error tracker that accepts the Sentry protocol, so existing Sentry SDKs can point at it by changing the DSN, and it also stores logs, transactions, release health and AI-agent traces.
summary.what_it_does: Accepts standard Sentry envelopes from any Sentry SDK and groups events into issues using a deterministic fingerprint. Runs as a single process with SQLite by default, serving both the API and a static dashboard, with PostgreSQL available via a separate compose file. Ingestion writes the envelope to disk and returns 200 before a spawned task does the database work. It also provides performance views with p95 ranking, structured logs with six severities, release health (crash-free sessions and users), and AI agent trace pages that read Sentry's Spans Protocol v2. Alert rules for new issues, regressions and unmutes can notify Slack, SMTP email or a JSON webhook. An optional built-in MCP endpoint lets AI assistants query the instance, and there is a typed TypeScript REST client.
use_cases: centralized application logs with trace links
alert team on new or regressed errors
how_to_run: Open the dashboard in a browser and sign in with the superuser credentials
Create a project, copy its DSN and set it in your Sentry SDK
notable: Speaks the Sentry protocol so existing Sentry SDKs work by changing the DSN
Single container with SQLite by default; dashboard served as static files by the same process
Two-phase ingestion: accepts events before database work
Built-in MCP endpoint for AI assistants
Reports exact AI token counts rather than cost estimates
caveats: Telemetry is on by default, sending an anonymous report every six hours unless disabled with RUSTRAK_TELEMETRY=off or DO_NOT_TRACK=1
Sponsorship-funded with no paid tier or hosted plan stated; the README does not describe a hosted service
Scale-out guidance points to PostgreSQL; the README does not give limits beyond the single benchmark (about 5k events/sec on a 4-core box with SQLite)
